QF.id: VIII Introduction to Clearing and Settlement System_11

question.text: A key advantage of SPAN margining over flat percentage-based margining is:

answer.text: SPAN recognizes the risk-reducing effect of hedged positions and charges lower margins for offset portfolios
SPAN always charges higher margins than flat percentage methods
SPAN is simpler to compute than flat percentage margins
SPAN does not require daily margin recalculation

explanation.text: The Logic: SPAN evaluates risk at the portfolio level rather than position by position. Because it re-prices the whole book under each risk scenario, naturally offsetting positions (for example a futures long combined with a long put) produce a smaller worst-case loss than either leg in isolation. In general industry use this means SPAN sets initial margin sufficient to cover the largest reasonably expected one-day portfolio loss while treating futures and options uniformly and recognising option-portfolio exposures. The Trap: SPAN is not simpler than flat percentage margining, it does not skip daily recalculation, and it does not unconditionally charge higher margins. Its distinguishing feature is portfolio-level treatment, not always-higher or always-lower margin. Note: The cited NISM-Series-VIII workbook pages (160-161) support SPAN as portfolio risk analysis and confirm uniform treatment of futures and options and recognition of option-portfolio exposures, but the specific comparison to flat percentage margining and the explicit "lower margin for hedged/offset portfolios" wording were not located in the pages checked. The framing above is general industry description of portfolio-based margining rather than a direct workbook citation.
